findings.description: `host.endswith(domain)` does not require a dot boundary. With partner domain `shop.example`, an attacker-controlled origin like `https://evilshop.example` or `https://notshop.example` passes. The API then reflects that origin with `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true`, so the attacker's site can read member balances and redeem rewards using the victim's session cookie.
findings.title: Partner domain check uses bare endswith, allowing look-alike origins with credentials

findings.description: The header reflects the request's original `origin` string. A trailing slash is stripped for the allow check but is still echoed back, so a request with `Origin: https://a.example/` gets `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: https://a.example/`. Browsers compare this to the serialized origin, which has no trailing slash, so the request would be blocked. The same applies to the preflight response at line 63.
findings.suggestion: Return the normalised origin, or the exact configured origin, in the header.
findings.title: Allow-Origin echoes the raw origin rather than the normalised one
